The Gibeonites' wrong is answered (verses 1–9)

All suffering arises from the entrance of sin into the world and should lead us to humility and repentance.

Some disasters especially call earlier sins to remembrance.

God's judgments may concern wrongdoing committed a long time before.

We should not object as though we understood all the reasons behind his governance.

The people's suffering for Saul's wrongdoing may have reflected their participation in it.

Likewise, a later generation may suffer consequences arising from an earlier generation's sins.

The passage does not disclose every reason, and God has not promised to explain every aspect of his providence.

Delay does not remove guilt.

Nor can sinners assume that because judgment has been postponed, they will escape it.

A financial payment could not satisfy the demand for justice after bloodshed.

Henry understands Saul's descendants as possibly having followed his violent example, since the family is described as a house of bloodshed.

He argues that the Gibeonites' demand was not driven by personal vengeance but by concern for public justice.

The sentence was carried out at the beginning of harvest.

Henry views it as an extraordinary judicial action under Israel's covenant order, intended to remove the judgment that had withheld productive harvests for years.

He argues that public penalties directed toward the common welfare should not automatically be condemned as cruelty.

This is his interpretation of an ancient historical judgment, not a contemporary authorization for collective punishment or private violence.

Rizpah honors the dead (verses 10–14)

When a guilty land has enjoyed many years of prosperity, its people should be thankful.

When abundance is misused, it is not surprising if scarcity follows.

Yet people often spend far more effort identifying physical causes of hardship than asking whether sin has contributed to their troubles.

The Lord defends the cause of those who cannot or will not avenge themselves.

The prayers of poor people are powerful.

When God sent rain upon the earth, the bodies were buried.

The rain showed that the Lord had heard prayer and granted mercy to the land.

Henry sees in these events a picture of Christ.

He was hung upon a tree and became a curse for us, removing our guilt though he himself was innocent.

Through him, God is reconciled to us.

David fights the Philistines (verses 15–22)

These events appear to have occurred near the end of David's reign.

David grew exhausted but did not flee.

The Lord provided help when he needed it.

Even strong believers sometimes grow weary in spiritual conflict.

Satan may attack them most fiercely at such moments.

But those who stand firm, resist him and trust the Lord will receive help.

At last they will become more than conquerors.

Death, the Christian's last enemy, is like a mighty descendant of Anak.

But through the One who has already triumphed on our behalf, believers will finally overcome even death itself.

Battles with the Philistines. | (15-22) |
Verses 1-9
Every affliction arises from sin, and should lead us to repent and humble ourselves before God; but some troubles especially show that they are sent to bring sin to remembrance. God's judgments often look a great way back, which requires us to do so, when we are under his rebukes. It is not for us to object against the people's smarting for the sin of their king; perhaps they helped him. Nor against this generation suffering for the sin of the last. God often visits the sins of the fathers upon the children, and he gives no account of any matters. Time does not wear out the guilt of sin; nor can we build hopes of escape upon the delay of judgments. If we cannot understand all the reasons of Providence in this matter, still we have no right to demand that God should acquaint us with those reasons. It must be right, because it is the will of God, and in the end it will be proved to be so. Money is no satisfaction for blood. It should seem, Saul's posterity trod in his steps, for it is called a bloody house. It was the spirit of the family, therefore they are justly reckoned with for his sin, as well as for their own. The Gibeonites did not require this out of malice against Saul or his family. It was not to gratify any revenge, but for the public good. They were put to death at the beginning of harvest; they were thus sacrificed to turn away the wrath of Almighty God, who had withheld the harvest-mercies for some years past, and to obtain his favour in the present harvest. In vain do we expect mercy from God, unless we do justice upon our sins. Executions must not be thought cruel, which are for the public welfare.
[2Sam.21.10-2Sam.21.14]
Verses 10-14
That a guilty land should enjoy many years of plenty, calls for gratitude; and we need not wonder misused abundance should be punished with scarcity; yet how few are disposed to ask of the Lord concerning the sinful cause, while numbers search for the second causes by which he is pleased to work! But the Lord will plead the cause of those who cannot or will not avenge themselves; and the prayers of the poor are of great power. When God sent rain to water the earth, these bodies were buried, for then it appeared that God was entreated for the land. When justice is done on earth, vengeance from heaven ceases. God is pacified, and is entreated for us through Christ, who was hanged on a tree, and so made a curse for us, to do away our guilt, though he was himself guiltless.
[2Sam.21.15-2Sam.21.22]
Verses 15-22
These events seem to have taken place towards the end of David's reign. David fainted, but he did not flee, and God sent help in the time of need. In spiritual conflicts, even strong saints sometimes wax faint; then Satan attacks them furiously; but those who stand their ground and resist him, shall be relieved and made more than conquerors. Death is a Christian's last enemy, and a son of Anak; but through Him that triumphed for us, believers shall be more than conquerors at last, even over that enemy.

Original heading

David's psalm of thanksgiving.

Praise for deliverance

This chapter is a psalm of praise.

Almost the same song appears later as Psalm 18.

Those who trust the Lord while walking in the path of duty will find him ready to help them in their greatest dangers.

David experienced this personally.

When God preserves us in a remarkable way, we should remember those particular mercies and mention them specifically when praising him.

We will not be completely delivered from every enemy until we reach heaven.

But God will preserve all his people until then (2 Timothy 4:18).

People who have received great mercy from God should give the glory to him.

David sang this song on the very day when the Lord delivered him.

While the mercy is still fresh and we are deeply moved by it, we should bring our offering of thanks.

The warmth of our gratitude can kindle the offering.

David's hopes and joys finally centered upon the great Redeemer.

All our own hopes should end in him as well.

--This chapter is a psalm of praise; we find it afterwards nearly as Psa 18. They that trust God in the way of duty, shall find him a present help in their greatest dangers: David did so. Remarkable preservations should be particularly mentioned in our praises. We shall never be delivered from all enemies till we get to heaven. God will preserve all his people, [2Tim.4.18] 2Ti 4:18. Those who receive signal mercies from God, ought to give him the glory. In the day that God delivered David, he sang this song. While the mercy is fresh, and we are most affected with it, let the thank-offering be brought, to be kindled with the fire of that affection. All his joys and hopes close, as all our hopes should do, in the great Redeemer.

David's final words (verses 1–7)

David's final testimony deserves serious attention.

Those who have spent many years enjoying God's goodness and finding wisdom in his ways should bear witness to the truth of his promises as their earthly lives draw to a close.

David declared that God had inspired his words.

The Holy Spirit spoke through him.

Like other holy men, he spoke and wrote as the Spirit moved him.

David had many failures to confess.

He had neglected duties and sometimes acted wrongly.

Yet he found comfort in the Lord's everlasting covenant with him.

Above all, David meant the covenant of mercy and peace.

He received it as a sinner who believed in the promised Savior, accepted God's promised blessing and surrendered himself to serve the Lord as someone redeemed by grace.

Believers will enjoy these covenant blessings forever.

God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit will receive eternal glory through their salvation.

Forgiveness, righteousness, grace and everlasting life are secured as God's gifts through Jesus Christ.

Christ possesses limitless riches of grace and every blessing for people who seek salvation through him.

David knew enough of the holy law to understand the greatness of his own sin.

He therefore knew how deeply he needed Christ's salvation.

The covenant was all his salvation and therefore all his desire.

Compared with this hope, every earthly thing became less attractive.

David was ready to surrender earthly things or leave them behind at death so that he could enjoy perfect happiness with God (Psalm 73:24–28).

Yet he grieved that sinful desires remained powerful within him and that his own faith, hope and love were often weak.

He would readily have admitted that his carelessness and lack of watchfulness had contributed to these weaknesses.

Nevertheless, the hope of being made perfect in heavenly glory encouraged him as he approached death.

David's mighty men (verses 8–39)

David once longed for water from the well at Bethlehem.

His desire seems to have been a moment of weakness.

Thirsty and remembering the water he had drunk there when he was young, he spoke without sufficient thought.

His mighty men were eager to risk their lives at even a slight suggestion from their king.

How much more eagerly should we seek to please the Lord Jesus, obeying his will as revealed through Scripture, the Holy Spirit and his providence!

But David refused to drink that water.

He poured it out to the Lord as a drink offering.

In this way he opposed his own foolish desire, disciplined himself for indulging it and showed that sober reflection could correct his rashness.

He understood the need for self-denial.

David treated that water as especially precious because his men had risked their blood to obtain it.

How much more highly should we value the blessings purchased for us through the blood of the Savior!

Let us not neglect so great a salvation.

[2Sam.23.1-2Sam.23.7]
Chapter 23
Chapter Outline
David's last words. | (1-7) |
David's mighty men. | (8-39) |
Verses 1-7
These words of David are very worthy of regard. Let those who have had long experience of God's goodness, and the pleasantness of heavenly wisdom, when they come to finish their course, bear their testimony to the truth of the promise. David avows his Divine inspiration, that the Spirit of God spake by him. He, and other holy men, spake and wrote as they were moved by the Holy Ghost. In many things he had his own neglect and wrong conduct to blame. But David comforted himself that the Lord had made with him an everlasting covenant. By this he principally intended the covenant of mercy and peace, which the Lord made with him as a sinner, who believed in the promised Saviour, who embraced the promised blessing, who yielded up himself to the Lord, to be his redeemed servant. Believers shall for ever enjoy covenant blessings; and God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, shall be for ever glorified in their salvation. Thus pardon, righteousness, grace, and eternal life, are secured as the gift of God through Jesus Christ. There is an infinite fulness of grace and all blessings treasured up in Christ, for those who seek his salvation. This covenant was all David's salvation, he so well knew the holy law of God and the extent of his own sinfulness, that he perceived what was needful for his own case in this salvation. It was therefore all his desire. In comparison, all earthly objects lost their attractions; he was willing to give them up, or to die and leave them, that he might enjoy full happiness, [Ps.73.24-Ps.73.28] Psa 73:24-28. Still the power of evil, and the weakness of his faith, hope, and love, were his grief and burden. Doubtless he would have allowed that his own slackness and want of care were the cause; but the hope that he should soon be made perfect in glory, encouraged him in his dying moments.
[2Sam.23.8-2Sam.23.39]
Verses 8-39
David once earnestly longed for the water at the well of Bethlehem. It seems to be an instance of weakness. He was thirsty; with the water of that well he had often refreshed himself when a youth, and it was without due thought that he desired it. Were his valiant men so forward to expose themselves, upon the least hint of their prince's mind, and so eager to please him, and shall not we long to approve ourselves to our Lord Jesus, by ready compliance with his will, as shown us by his word, Spirit, and providence? But David poured out the water as a drink-offering to the Lord. Thus he would cross his own foolish fancy, and punish himself for indulging it, and show that he had sober thoughts to correct his rash ones, and knew how to deny himself. Did David look upon that water as very precious which was got at the hazard of these men's blood, and shall not we much more value those benefits for purchasing which our blessed Saviour shed his blood? Let all beware of neglecting so great salvation.

David orders a census (verses 1–9)

Because Israel had sinned, God allowed David to act wrongly.

The people then shared in the punishment that followed.

This teaches something important about God's government of the world.

The sin was the pride in David's heart.

By counting the nation, he hoped to appear more powerful and intimidating.

He trusted human strength more than he should have done, although he had written so often about trusting God alone.

The Lord does not judge sins as we do.

An act that appears to us harmless, or at worst a small mistake, may be deeply sinful before him.

God searches the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

Sometimes even ungodly people recognize wrong attitudes or behavior in believers when those believers remain unaware of them.

Yet God rarely allows those he loves to enjoy for long the things they selfishly covet.

David chooses the plague (verses 10–15)

It is good for us when, after sinning, our consciences convict us.

When we confess our sins, we may pray with faith for forgiveness and for God's mercy to remove the guilt we abandon through sincere repentance.

It is just for God to take away what we boast about, or turn it into something bitter, so that our pride becomes a source of correction.

The punishment involved the people as well as David.

Although David's sin opened the way for judgment, the people's own sins also contributed.

David chose a judgment that would come directly from God.

He knew God's mercies were very great.

He preferred this to falling into the hands of enemies who would rejoice at Israel's suffering and become further hardened in their idolatry.

The plague would place David and his family in as much danger as the poorest Israelite.

It would also last for a shorter time than the other offered judgments, however severe its effects.

The rapid destruction showed how easily God can bring down the proud and how much we owe each day to his patience.

God stops the destroying angel (verses 16 and 17)

Henry suggests that Jerusalem may have been especially guilty of sin and pride, leading the destroying angel to stretch out his hand toward that city.

But God relented.

As elsewhere, Henry explains that this means a change in God's manner of dealing with people, not a change in his eternal mind.

At the place where Abraham had been prevented from killing his son, the destroying angel was likewise stopped from destroying Jerusalem.

It is because of the great Sacrifice, Jesus Christ, that lives otherwise forfeited are protected from final destruction.

David showed a true shepherd's heart by offering to bear the judgment himself in order to save his subjects.

David offers sacrifices; the plague ends (verses 18–25)

God's encouragement to offer him spiritual sacrifices is a sign that he is bringing us into fellowship with himself.

David purchased the ground on which he would build an altar.

God hates offerings acquired by injustice.

People who care chiefly about making their religion easy and inexpensive, involving little effort or money, do not understand true devotion.

What else are our possessions for, if not to honor God?

How could they be put to better use?

David offered burnt offerings, expressing honor for God's justice, and fellowship offerings, expressing honor for his mercy.

Christ is both our Altar and our Sacrifice.

Only through him can we expect to escape God's righteous judgment and receive his favor.

Death is destroying people all around us through many different causes, often suddenly.

It is foolish not to expect our own death and prepare to meet God.

He chooses the pestilence. | (10-15) |
The staying the pestilence. | (16-17) |
David's sacrifice, The plague removed. | (18-25) |
Verses 1-9
For the people's sin David was left to act wrong, and in his chastisement they received punishment. This example throws light upon God's government of the world, and furnishes a useful lesson. The pride of David's heart, was his sin in numbering of the people. He thought thereby to appear the more formidable, trusting in an arm of flesh more than he should have done, and though he had written so much of trusting in God only. God judges not of sin as we do. What appears to us harmless, or, at least, but a small offence, may be a great sin in the eye of God, who discerns the thoughts and intents of the heart. Even ungodly men can discern evil tempers and wrong conduct in believers, of which they themselves often remain unconscious. But God seldom allows those whom he loves the pleasures they sinfully covet.
[2Sam.24.10-2Sam.24.15]
Verses 10-15
It is well, when a man has sinned, if he has a heart within to smite him for it. If we confess our sins, we may pray in faith that God would forgive them, and take away, by pardoning mercy, that sin which we cast away by sincere repentance. What we make the matter of our pride, it is just in God to take from us, or make bitter to us, and make it our punishment. This must be such a punishment as the people have a large share in, for though it was David's sin that opened the sluice, the sins of the people all contributed to the flood. In this difficulty, David chose a judgment which came immediately from God, whose mercies he knew to be very great, rather than from men, who would have triumphed in the miseries of Israel, and have been thereby hardened in their idolatry. He chose the pestilence; he and his family would be as much exposed to it as the poorest Israelite; and he would continue for a shorter time under the Divine rebuke, however severe it was. The rapid destruction by the pestilence shows how easily God can bring down the proudest sinners, and how much we owe daily to the Divine patience.
[2Sam.24.16-2Sam.24.17]
Verses 16-17
Perhaps there was more wickedness, especially more pride, and that was the sin now chastised, in Jerusalem than elsewhere, therefore the hand of the destroyer is stretched out upon that city; but the Lord repented him of the evil, changed not his mind, but his way. In the very place where Abraham was stayed from slaying his son, this angel, by a like countermand, was stayed from destroying Jerusalem. It is for the sake of the great Sacrifice, that our forfeited lives are preserved from the destroying angel. And in David is the spirit of a true shepherd of the people, offering himself as a sacrifice to God, for the salvation of his subjects.
[2Sam.24.18-2Sam.24.25]
Verses 18-25
God's encouraging us to offer to him spiritual sacrifices, is an evidence of his reconciling us to himself. David purchased the ground to build the altar. God hates robbery for burnt-offering. Those know not what religion is, who chiefly care to make it cheap and easy to themselves, and who are best pleased with that which costs them least pains or money. For what have we our substance, but to honour God with it; and how can it be better bestowed? See the building of the altar, and the offering proper sacrifices upon it. Burnt-offerings to the glory of God's justice; peace-offerings to the glory of his mercy. Christ is our Altar, our Sacrifice; in him alone we may expect to escape his wrath, and to find favour with God. Death is destroying all around, in so many forms, and so suddenly, that it is madness not to expect and prepare for the close of life.
